lead: Every security requirement you meet this year is one of three promises about data and service. Keep the data secret — confidentiality. Keep the data correct — integrity. Keep the service reachable — availability. A UPI payment shows all three at once: the amount must stay private, must not change in transit, and the bank's server must answer before the app times out. Engineers call these the CIA triad. Almost every exam question about a security incident is really asking which of the three broke.

blocks.text: Confidentiality means only allowed parties can read the data. A UPI payment leaves your phone carrying the payee address, the amount and an encrypted PIN block. On a shop's open Wi-Fi, a sniffer can read every field the app fails to encrypt. Confidentiality is the promise that it cannot.

Integrity means the data is exactly what the sender wrote. A mark sheet row says 18 out of 20 and someone edits it to 20. Nothing crashes, no error is shown, the record simply says something else. Integrity fails when a change happens and nobody detects it.

Availability means the service answers when a real user needs it. Tatkal opens at 10:00 and lakhs of people refresh the IRCTC page at that second; the site must still take bookings. Availability fails when the service is slow, down or unreachable.
A control usually protects one goal and costs another. The next chapter separates what you promise (a service) from the tool that delivers it (a mechanism).

sections.h3: The extra goals and the DAD set

blocks.text: Some syllabi list three more goals beside CIA.

items: Authentication: each party proves who it is before the exchange. Your app verifies the bank's certificate; you prove yourself with a PIN.
Accountability: every action is traceable to a named entity. The bank log shows which employee opened which account, and when.
Non-repudiation: a party cannot later deny an action it really did. A digitally signed payment instruction cannot be waved away as 'I never sent that'.

blocks.text: The mirror image of CIA is the failure set some syllabi call DAD: disclosure breaks confidentiality, alteration breaks integrity, destruction (or denial) breaks availability. Describe an attack by the goal it breaks and the marking becomes easy.

sections.h3: Controls trade off, and trust must be stated

blocks.text: Controls compete for the same resources. Encrypting every field of a payment request protects confidentiality, but CPU cost per request rises, queues grow, and at peak the service slows — availability drops. Locking an account after three wrong PINs stops guessing, but an attacker who knows your username can lock you out on purpose. Security is a balance, not a maximum.
The balance is written down as a trust and threat model. It answers four questions.

items: Who is trusted: users, admins, the cloud provider, the certificate authority.
What each trusted party can do: read a row, sign a certificate, restart a server.
What you assume they will not do: steal data, collude, or make careless mistakes.
What happens when an assumption is false: a lost admin laptop counts as a disclosure event.

sections.h3: Confidentiality matrix and uptime as a number

blocks.text: A confidentiality determination matrix lists assets against data classes and records who may read each one. Build it before choosing controls: a Restricted row needs encryption at rest, a Public row does not. Keep it short, one line per asset.
Availability is quoted as a percentage over a stated period, never as the sentence 'the server is up'.

blocks.where: A is availability in percent; T is the total minutes in the stated period (days × 24 × 60); D is the minutes the service was unusable.

figure.caption: Over 30 days (43,200 minutes) the portal was down for 108 minutes, so its availability is 43,092 ÷ 43,200 = 99.75%. The other three events each touch one named goal.

spec.aria: Thirty day cells with one thin red sliver, an enlarged day bar showing 108 of 1,440 minutes down, the availability formula, and three chips naming integrity, confidentiality, and authentication with non-repudiation.

examples.question: A college result portal must run continuously for 30 days. (a) It was unusable for 108 minutes. Compute its availability. (b) A student edits his own marks row directly in the database. (c) A mark sheet PDF is readable by anyone holding the link, with no login. (d) Only exam-cell staff can publish results, and each publish is digitally signed. Name the goal broken or provided in (b), (c) and (d).
steps: (a) Total minutes in the stated period: T = 30 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes = 43200 minutes.
(b) The record changed and nobody detected it: integrity is broken.
(c) Data is readable by people who were never authorised: confidentiality is broken.
(d) Staff identity is proved, and a signature stops later denial: authentication and non-repudiation are provided.
examples.answer: Availability is 99.75% over 30 days; (b) breaks integrity, (c) breaks confidentiality, and (d) provides authentication and non-repudiation.
examples.check:
total = 30 * 24 * 60
up = total - 108
avail = up / total * 100
print(total)
print(up)
print(round(avail, 2))

traps: Writing 'security means confidentiality'. Marks come from naming the goal a stated incident broke: a crash is availability, a silent edit is integrity, a leak is confidentiality.
Quoting availability as 'the server is up'. It is a percentage over a declared period, so always write the period and the down minutes.
Assuming encryption gives integrity. It hides data from outsiders; a party who holds the key can still change it undetected. Detecting change needs a MAC or a signature (see Unit 4).
Treating authentication and non-repudiation as one idea. A shared password authenticates but can be denied later; a digital signature cannot.
Mismatching the DAD set. Disclosure pairs with confidentiality, alteration with integrity, destruction with availability — never cross them.

quiz.q: Define the three goals of the CIA triad in one line each.
quiz.a: Confidentiality: only authorised parties can read the data. Integrity: the data is not changed undetected. Availability: the service is usable when an authorised user needs it.

quiz.q: A student changes his own marks row in the college database, and no outsider ever reads the table. Which goal fails, and why not confidentiality?
quiz.a: Integrity fails, because the stored value no longer matches what the examiner recorded and nothing detected the change. Confidentiality is untouched: no unauthorised party gained read access.

quiz.q: A booking server must run for 7 days and was unusable for 20 minutes. Compute availability in percent.

A bank adds heavy field-level encryption to every login request. At peak load the login page takes 12 seconds instead of 3, and users give up. Which goal is being traded away, and against which benefit?
quiz.a: Availability is traded away: the service is technically up but too slow to use, so availability in the stated period falls. The benefit is confidentiality of the fields in transit. The fix is to encrypt selectively or add capacity, not to remove the control.

quiz.q: Classify these three assets in a confidentiality determination matrix and name the class for each: a published timetable PDF, an internal staff salary sheet, and the encryption keys of the exam server.
quiz.a: Timetable PDF: Public, anyone may read it. Salary sheet: Internal, staff and HR only. Encryption keys: Restricted, key custodians only.

quiz.q: Give the DAD failure that corresponds to each CIA goal.
quiz.a: Confidentiality — disclosure. Integrity — alteration. Availability — destruction (denial).

quiz.q: Only exam-cell staff may publish results, and each publish is digitally signed. Which two goals beyond CIA does this provide, and what does each one stop?
quiz.a: Authentication stops an outsider posing as staff, because identity is proved before publishing. Non-repudiation stops a staff member later denying that he published, because the signature is bound to him. Accountability follows if every publish is also logged with a name and time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry writes the CIA triad into service contracts: a cloud provider's SLA states uptime as a percentage over a month with listed exclusions, and the shared-responsibility model splits the three goals between provider and customer. Regulators publish cyber-security frameworks that restate the same three promises as mandatory controls for banks and payment apps. Zero-trust architecture attacks the trust model itself, assuming the internal network is already hostile. Search next for zero trust, SLA uptime clauses, and confidentiality classification matrices.
